title: Exploring the Effects of Generative AI Assistance on Writing Self-efficacy
venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '26)
extended_summary:
This pilot study examines how different configurations of generative AI assistance affect students’ writing self-efficacy during argumentative writing. Rather than asking whether AI helps in general, the paper focuses on where in the writing process AI intervenes—idea generation, sentence construction, both, or neither—and whether those different forms of support shape confidence, agency, and perceived writing ability differently.

The intervention used ChatGPT in a 2 × 2 between-subjects experimental design crossing AI support for idea generation and AI support for text construction. This created four conditions: No AI, Sentence AI, Ideation AI, and Full AI. Participants completed two 30-minute argumentative essay tasks in Korean during a 100-minute online session, with post-task self-efficacy surveys after each task. The study also reviewed participant reflections and ChatGPT interaction logs descriptively to contextualize the quantitative patterns.

The population consisted of 13 Korean undergraduate students, recruited voluntarily, after 8 of 21 initial recruits were excluded for non-attendance or procedural noncompliance. The study was conducted online via Google Meet in South Korea, using the free web version of ChatGPT. The primary measured outcome was writing self-efficacy, assessed on a 0–100 self-report scale covering writing ability, process management, and writing experience.

The main conclusion is that generative AI did not have uniform effects: outcomes depended strongly on the configuration of support. Full AI support produced the highest but largely stable self-efficacy, yet participants also reported diminished ownership and authenticity. Ideation-level AI showed the most promising pattern, combining high self-efficacy with positive change over time and preserved learner agency. Sentence-level AI showed a concerning pattern of universal self-efficacy decline across participants, suggesting that revision-focused support may undermine confidence when it functions as a comparative standard. The authors frame the study as preliminary and argue that future larger-scale, longitudinal research is needed to test whether these configuration-specific effects persist.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a small pilot experimental study with n=13 undergraduate participants, exploratory analyses, wide uncertainty, and no direct K-12 sample. It has clearer methodology than opinion pieces but does not meet strong causal evidence standards for the target K-12 question.
impact_tier_rationale: Reported effects on self-efficacy are suggestive and sometimes large in magnitude, but estimates are unstable, confidence intervals include zero, and literacy performance impacts are not directly measured. Overall impact is therefore unclear rather than clearly positive or null.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT configured as a writing assistant for undergraduate argumentative writing, with condition-specific support for ideation only, sentence-level drafting/revision, or full-process writing assistance.
Conversational use of ChatGPT through prompt-constrained dialogue to support brainstorming and/or text revision during essay writing tasks.

finding.finding_summary: This pilot experiment examined writing self-efficacy across four ChatGPT assistance configurations in 13 Korean undergraduates. Full AI support showed higher average self-efficacy than no AI (M=82.2 vs. 61.8; g=1.23, 95% CI [-0.60, 3.07]) and higher than sentence-level AI (g=0.73), but confidence intervals spanned zero and authors emphasize the study was underpowered. Over time, ideation-only AI showed the largest within-person gain (ΔM=+11.1, SD=16.2), full AI was stable (ΔM=+0.5, SD=6.7), no AI changed little (ΔM=+1.3, SD=2.4), and sentence-level AI declined for all five participants (ΔM=-5.7, SD=5.6).
finding.measure: Post-task writing self-efficacy ratings on a 0-100 scale across writing ability, process management, and writing experience subdomains
finding.effect_size: g=1.23 (Full AI vs No AI); g=0.73 (Full AI vs Sentence AI); g=0.99 (Sentence AI vs No AI); g=0.31 (Ideation AI vs Sentence AI)
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CI [-0.60, 3.07] for Full AI vs No AI; other CIs not_reported
finding.std_deviation: Full AI SD=6.4; Ideation AI SD=16.1; Sentence AI SD=7.2; No AI SD=24.0; change-score SDs: 16.2, 6.7, 5.6, 2.4

finding.finding_summary: The paper is about AI-assisted argumentative writing, but it does not directly measure writing quality, revision quality, reading, vocabulary, or error reduction as literacy outcomes. Literacy-relevant evidence is indirect through self-efficacy items about grammar correction, vocabulary choice, coherence, evidence use, and writing to task; qualitative observations suggest ideation support preserved personal voice while full AI reduced ownership, but no rubric-scored product outcomes were reported.
finding.measure: Self-perceived writing ability and qualitative reflections, not externally assessed literacy performance

finding.finding_summary: The study reports exploratory evidence relevant to learner agency and independent problem-solving rather than direct performance transfer. Participants in the ideation AI condition reported writing in their own language and showed positive self-efficacy trajectories, whereas full AI users reported reduced ownership and one no-AI participant who habitually used AI struggled to write independently when support was removed; however, no formal transfer task or post-removal performance measure was administered.
finding.measure: Self-efficacy items on independent resolution of writing difficulties and qualitative observations about ownership/agency
